title: Forest garden: the herbaceous layer
subtitle: Perennial herbs and vegetables for the 0 to 0.5 m band in a forest garden.
excerpt: The herbaceous layer in a forest garden is everything from ground level to about 50 cm: perennial herbs, edible flowers, and dynamic accumulators that fill the space between shrubs and under the canopy edge. This layer is where most of the maintenance work happens.
sourceNotes: Layer framework from Martin Crawford, Creating a Forest Garden (2010). Species selection from Plants For A Future database (pfaf.org). Management notes from Agroforestry Research Trust trial data.

glossaryTerms.definition: In a forest garden, the plants that grow from ground level to about 50 cm in height: perennial herbs, edible groundcover, and dynamic accumulators that fill the space between woody shrubs. The herbaceous layer is usually the most diverse and the most actively managed part of the system.

content.text: fills the ground between shrubs and trees in a forest garden. It is more diverse than the other layers and needs more management: cutting back fast spreaders, dividing clumps, and ensuring no single plant takes over. The goal is a stable, self-managing mix, but it takes five to seven years of active work to get there.
Core plants for the herbaceous layer

Comfrey is indispensable: cut three or four times per year for chop-and-drop mulch. Yarrow provides flowers for predatory insects and acts as a dynamic accumulator. Sorrel gives a persistent harvest in shade. Mints fill gaps under shrubs but must be managed to prevent them spreading too far.

Good King Henry, sorrel, lovage, sweet cicely, and Welsh onion all suit the herbaceous layer. Place shade-tolerant plants (sorrel, sweet cicely) under the canopy edge. Place plants that need more sun (lovage, Welsh onion) where the canopy opens or at the south-facing edge of the system.

Cut back the whole layer once a year, in early spring before new growth starts. This removes dead material, checks spreading plants, and resets the light balance. In summer, spot-cut any plant that is crowding its neighbours. Top-dress annually with compost where the soil is bare.
